A Shared Filesystem gives your sandboxes and workflow tasks the same persistent files, so parallel agents can read shared inputs, write their own outputs, and build on each other's work. Files stay put after the compute that used them shuts down. Request early access. [...] Today we’re launching Render Sandboxes in public beta. Render Sandboxes let you safely give your agents a computer to work with: a fully isolated Linux environment where they can install dependencies, edit files, and run code.

Each sandbox starts quickly, runs indefinitely, and automatically suspends when idle. You can reliably run thousands at once and lock down what each one can reach. You’re billed for CPU only when your agents are actually using it.

Render Sandboxes work with any agent harness and model. You can operate sandboxes through the TypeScript or Python SDK, or the Render CLI.

Check out our quickstart, or share this prompt with your coding agent:

## Agents need a computer of their own [...] ## Agents need a computer of their own

Agents doing complex work need a separate machine for each task or user, isolated from your app and from each other. And since agent work comes in bursts, those machines need to start and stop with demand.

A web service isn’t built for this. Its instances stay up and serve all your users, and a new deploy can take minutes.

Render Sandboxes give each user or task its own machine the moment it’s needed. Each sandbox runs in its own Firecracker microVM.

results.title: Give your agent its own computer
results.content:
## LangSmith Sandboxes: a computer for every agent

The mental model that helps here: a sandbox needs to be two things at once. It needs the instant startup of a serverless function because you can't make an agent wait two minutes for a VM to boot. And it needs the statefulness of a full machine because agents aren't stateless request-handlers; they're mid-session workers that install dependencies, edit files, and pick up where they left off.

LangSmith Sandboxes are built for that model. Each one is a hardware-virtualized microVM. Not a container, a full machine with its own kernel. The agent gets:

```

Agent └── its own computer ├── filesystem ├── shell ├── package manager ├── network access ├── code execution └── persistent state
``` [...] LLMs can reason. But reasoning alone doesn't get much done.

Running code execution in an AI agent is harder than it looks. Your agent needs a real computer (filesystem, shell, package manager, persistent state) but handing it access to your infrastructure is dangerous.

Think about it this way: you use one laptop. You are n of one. But agents are going to run millions of tasks, and each one needs its own computer to work from. That's the infrastructure shift happening right now. Satya Nadella put it plainly: "Every agent needs a computer." The question is what that computer looks like, and how you give it to them safely.

LangSmith Sandboxes are our answer to that. Here's why it matters, and why doing it yourself is harder than it sounds.

results.title: Render just removed its AI sandbox time limit — and Vercel still has a 24-hour cap - The New Stack
results.content:
A risk remains if a process crashes after a payment goes through but before the result is saved. Render recommends using idempotency keys to prevent duplicate charges or database writes. Shared Filesystems let sandboxes and workflow tasks access the same persistent files, even after the compute that created them shuts down.

Render says the feature is designed for “many agents reading the same repo or dataset, with each one writing its own output.” But handling “concurrent writes to the same file, including locking and conflict resolution, is something we’re still studying,” the company tells The New Stack. [...] The bigger difference comes when a sandbox needs to resume work. Vercel limits uninterrupted sessions to 24 hours, and while persistent sandboxes can restart, their running processes start over.

Render takes a different approach. A sandbox “suspends when it goes idle and wakes on the next command with its files and memory intact, so the agent picks up mid-task instead of rebuilding its state,” the company tells The New Stack.
